name: Mark Zuckerberg
role: American technology entrepreneur; co-founder and CEO of Facebook/Meta (2004–present)
summary: A technology executive who has never declared a party affiliation and whose public political record centres on immigration reform, free expression online, privacy and technology optimism. In the 2010s he advocated expansive immigration, open trade, global cooperation and a stronger safety net including exploring a basic income; from 2024 he moved closer to the Trump administration, emphasised resisting government pressure on speech and was reported to describe himself privately as libertarian or classical liberal. On many social and economic questions he has taken no clear public position.

universal-healthcare.rationale: He called for health care not tied to one employer (2017), which concerns portability rather than government-provided universal coverage. No clear position found.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: No direct public statement found; a reported private self-description as libertarian is not enough to record a position.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: In 2017 he said wealth inequality 'hurts everyone' and that giving everyone the freedom to pursue purpose 'isn't free. People like me should pay for it.' He also funded a California initiative to tax commercial property at market value. No later restatement found.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Mixed: in 2019 he called for clearer rules and new institutions for the internet, but he has opposed EU regulation of American tech companies. No general position on corporate regulation.

cut-welfare.rationale: He argued for a stronger cushion for everyone, including exploring a universal basic income and affordable child care, the opposite of cutting welfare.

surveillance-ok.rationale: He has championed encryption and data protection, but no direct statement on government anti-terror surveillance was found.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: He noted approvingly that American law does not treat hate speech as a category and argued that suppressing speech is more dangerous to democracy than almost any speech, while his platform removes hate speech that could lead to violence. His 2024–2025 moves against government pressure on speech point the same way.

strong-leader.rationale: He named 'the forces of authoritarianism' among those his generation must resist (2017); not a direct statement on bypassing gridlock.

empower-police-military.rationale: No general position found; his 2017 remark concerned focusing immigration enforcement on real threats.

rehabilitation.rationale: No statement by him found in the sources consulted.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: No statement by him found in the sources consulted.

more-religion-public.rationale: He has said religion is personally very important to him, but no position on its public role was found.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Mixed and indirect record (2016 rebuke of employees who crossed out 'Black Lives Matter'; later corporate retreat from diversity programmes). No clear personal policy position.

reduce-immigration.rationale: He founded the immigration-reform lobby FWD.us (2013), criticised the 2017 entry restrictions, and urged staying open to refugees and not targeting undocumented people who pose no threat. He grouped immigration with knowledge and trade as flows to be defended against those who would slow them.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: He favours global community in general terms, but no position on the UN or similar bodies was found.

free-trade.rationale: He framed the struggle of his era as 'forces for the flow of knowledge, trade, and immigration against those who would slow them down' (2017).

nation-first.rationale: In 2017 he opposed 'isolationism and nationalism' in favour of global community. Since 2024 he has aligned with the Trump administration on pushing back against foreign tech regulation, so the current position is less clear.

open-borders.rationale: Supports expansive immigration but no statement on eventually open borders was found.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: He named 'stopping climate change before we destroy the planet' as a generational project (2017), without specifying the role of government.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: His speeches present technology and connecting people as drivers of progress that decentralise power; his philanthropy funds science aimed at curing disease. Not a claim that tech solves most problems.

expand-nuclear.rationale: No statement by him found in the sources consulted.

experts-over-public.rationale: He said people, not tech companies, should decide what is credible, but this concerns online speech, not policy-making.

basic-income.rationale: 'We should explore ideas like universal basic income to give everyone a cushion to try new things' (2017): supportive, but framed as something to explore.

one-party-rule.rationale: He contrasts China's internet values with American ones, but no direct statement on one-party rule was found.

democracy-best.rationale: He has spoken of protecting democracy through free expression and of 'modernizing democracy so everyone can vote online', and opposes authoritarianism.

direct-votes.rationale: His call for online voting concerns access to voting, not direct legislation.

equal-outcomes.rationale: He criticised wealth inequality and stressed equal opportunity, but did not endorse equality of outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: His 2017 quiet-title suits against Native Hawaiian landholders, later dropped with regret, are a personal dispute rather than a stated policy position.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: No recorded position found; his techno-optimism suggests disagreement but no direct statement.

accelerate-technology.rationale: He praises entrepreneurship and 'the freedom to fail' as how progress is made, and accepts that automation will replace tens of millions of jobs while proposing a cushion rather than slowing it. Inferred, not stated directly.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: He committed Meta's messaging services to end-to-end encryption that 'prevents anyone — including us' from seeing content, and praised strong encryption for protecting protesters. He has not addressed government access in those terms directly.

notes: Most of his explicit policy statements date from 2013–2019 (FWD.us, the 2017 Harvard speech, the 2019 Georgetown speech). From 2024 he moved closer to Donald Trump, said he regretted yielding to Biden-administration pressure on COVID-19 content, stopped funding election infrastructure, and was reported to privately describe himself as libertarian or classical liberal; he has not publicly retracted the earlier positions recorded here, but answers on taxation, nationalism and the safety net rest on 2017 statements. Born 14 May 1984; living.
